lines.text: Suppose Earth were twice as wide. Same rock, same oceans, same air, just twice the planet.

Twice as wide sounds like a big change. It's much bigger than that. Make a cube twice as wide, and you need two layers of four: eight of the small ones. Balls work the same way. A ball twice as wide holds eight times as much stuff. So this Earth would have eight times the mass, and the ground would pull on you twice as hard.

By the top of this ladder, the air will be squeezed against the ground, the mountains will have sunk, and getting a rocket into space will take seven times the fuel. And at the very end, we'll find out why a planet this size probably wouldn't look like Earth at all.

We won't jump straight there. We'll grow the planet one rung at a time, and watch what breaks first. One rule: the rock stays the same, so the planet's pull grows exactly as fast as its size. First rung: ten percent bigger.
